r: This one-credit gateway course surveys hotel, restaurant, tourism, and event operations, development, and management, plus career pathways across the four professions. The applied work is synthesizing and explaining industry structure and interrelations, a knowledge-transmission task that observed-usage data places squarely inside the Computer & Mathematical and writing-heavy categories where AI use is already concentrated. No embodied service delivery or licensure requirement attaches to this orientation course itself, and it is not a hard prerequisite gate, though it functions as the program's foundational on-ramp. At 24 months, general-purpose models already summarize industry sectors and career paths competently, but near-term diffusion into curriculum design is limited, and the course's foundational orientation role still supports the instrumental case at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate industry overviews, career-pathway explanations, and operations summaries comparable to what this course delivers, and task-exposure research classifies this kind of synthesis and exposition among the more automatable categories. The course's gateway role no longer caps the rating past the near term, since the foundational-scaffolding protection applies only at 24 months under the deterministic rule. Nothing embodied, licensed, or credit-hour-mandated protects the content at this horizon, and diffusion of AI-assisted curriculum tools into gateway coursework is plausibly further along by this point than it is today. The rating rises to High: the applied explanatory and survey work the course performs is substantially reproducible by AI with limited human input, even though a live classroom retains value for orienting a cohort of majors to a shared program identity.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing essentially all of the descriptive, industry-survey synthesis this course covers, with no embodiment, licensure, or enduring foundational cap holding it back. The rating stays High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty about how hospitality programs restructure orientation coursework and about whether cohort-building and advising functions keep a live, in-person version of this course administratively necessary even as its informational content is fully AI-reproducible. The instrumental case for acquiring this specific overview knowledge from a human-led course is substantially eroded; what plausibly persists is the socialization and advising function, which is adjacent to but distinct from the instrumental knowledge-transfer question this rating scores, and that residual function is not itself sufficient to pull the rating back down.
HTE 1030.d: In this course, students are provided an overview of the hotel, restaurant, tourism, and event industries. Basic operations, development, and management of those industries are covered. The course includes career opportunities and industry interrelations across these four professions.

r: The course pairs document-production tasks — cover letters, scholarship applications, SWOT self-appraisals — with live components: interviewing-skills practice and a culminating departmental career expo where students apply learned skills in person. Cover-letter and self-appraisal drafting are writing tasks that task-exposure research classifies as highly exposed, and productivity studies show AI drafting assistance delivering large quality and speed gains on exactly this kind of document. But the graded competence also includes real-time interview performance and in-person networking at the expo, an embodied and interpersonal activity that dampens the rating one band under the deterministic rule. At 24 months the instrumental need to practice live interviewing and attend the expo in person keeps the rating at Low despite highly exposed document-drafting content.

By 2031, AI will draft polished cover letters, scholarship essays, and self-appraisals essentially on demand, further eroding the instrumental rationale for a course to teach students how to produce those documents themselves. What survives is the embodied, presence-dependent core: live interview performance under evaluation and in-person networking at the career expo, where a jagged-frontier gap between simulated practice and real interpersonal reading of a room persists. The base automatability rises with document-task exposure, but the interpersonal-presence dampener continues to hold the rating down one band, and no licensure or accreditation mandate exists to add a further cap in either direction. The rating moves to Medium: most of the course's written-deliverable content is AI-reproducible, while its live-practice core is not, producing a mixed but net-moderate erosion.

A decade out, AI-assisted document preparation is pervasive and unremarkable, and the instrumental case for teaching resume and cover-letter mechanics is substantially diminished. The live interview-practice and expo-networking components, however, remain genuinely embodied, real-time interpersonal activities that this rating's framework treats as resistant to substitution regardless of how capable drafting tools become, since presence and live social reading are the graded skill, not the paperwork surrounding it. The rating holds Medium, hedged by real uncertainty over how career-services pedagogy itself evolves — programs may lean further into live practice specifically because the written-document skill is now assumed rather than taught. The honest read is that document generation is nearly fully eroded while interview and networking competence remains a live, human-taught core.
HTE 1035.d: In this course, students gain an overview of the Hospitality, Tourism and Events Department at MSU Denver and learn how to maneuver through the University systems to become a successful student. The course includes career self-appraisal, academic management, scholarship application processing, cover letter instruction, interviewing skills, and strengths weakness opportunities threats analyses. At the conclusion of the semester, students attend a departmental career expo where students apply skills learned in class.

r: This three-credit fundamentals course fuses industry-overview content (hotel, restaurant, tourism, event operations and management) with career-development tasks — self-appraisal, scholarship and cover-letter drafting, SWOT analysis, and interview preparation — but unlike the standalone career course, it names no live expo or graded interview performance, so the interpersonal weight is lighter and does not trigger a full embodiment dampener. Both halves are knowledge-and-document tasks: explanatory synthesis and text drafting, both classified by task-exposure research as highly automatable. Census BTOS data shows AI firm adoption still under a fifth of firms as of late 2025, meaning near-term classroom and curricular diffusion still lags raw model capability. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI already performs the underlying synthesis and drafting tasks competently, but realized curricular displacement remains partial.

By 2031, AI will competently generate the industry synthesis and the personal career documents this fundamentals course teaches students to produce, and no embodiment, licensure, or credit-hour mandate binds the content. The foundational-gateway protection that holds the rating down at 24 months no longer applies under the deterministic rule past that horizon, since it caps only the first horizon. Observed-usage data already shows office and writing tasks concentrated in AI use, and that trend is expected to deepen further as diffusion catches up with capability. The rating rises to High: the applied explanatory and document-drafting work is substantially reproducible with limited human input, leaving the course's residual value concentrated in cohort orientation and advising rather than in content a model cannot already produce.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing nearly all of the descriptive and document-drafting tasks that make up this fundamentals course, with nothing in the catalog record — no clinical hours, no licensure board, no strict foundational lock — holding the rating down. It stays High, hedged by the same ten-year uncertainty that applies to any single-course prediction: hospitality programs could restructure gateway coursework around AI-assisted planning tools rather than eliminate it outright, and cohort-building functions may persist independent of the content's exposure level. The instrumental case for learning this specific overview-and-career content from a human-led course is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory, even if the course's convening function proves durable and its scheduling survives curricular revision.
HTE 1040.d: In this course, students are provided an overview of the hotel, restaurant, tourism and event industries. Basic operations, development, and management of those industries are covered. The course includes career opportunities and industry interrelations across these four professions. Students gain an overview of the Hospitality, Tourism and Events Department at MSU Denver, and learn how to maneuver through the university systems to become a successful student. The course includes career self-appraisal, academic management, scholarship application processing, cover letter instruction, interviewing skills, and strengths weakness opportunities threats analyses.

r: The course's applied competence is the interpersonal, intercultural, and nonverbal delivery of customer service: reading the service cycle, recognizing critical points of service, and reacting to a guest in real time, alongside designing and evaluating service systems and training staff to deliver them. The delivery core maps directly to the low-exposure, embodied interpersonal categories task-exposure research identifies, since nonverbal cues and live guest interaction are not text-generation tasks a model performs on a student's behalf. Some administrative layer — drafting service-evaluation rubrics or training materials — is exposed, but it is a modest fraction of the content. At 24 months the instrumental need to personally learn and practice live service delivery is intact; nothing in current AI deployment substitutes for it.

By 2031, AI tools will likely draft training materials, service-standard documentation, and evaluation rubrics competently, nudging the administrative layer of this course toward automation. But the graded core — a student's capacity to read nonverbal cues, manage a live service cycle, and adapt intercultural communication in real time with a guest — remains an embodied, presence-dependent competence that the jagged-frontier finding suggests AI performs poorly outside carefully bounded contexts, with real risk if trusted uncritically in live guest interactions where nonverbal misread has immediate consequences. No licensure or accreditation mandate applies, but embodiment alone is doing the protective work here. The rating holds Low: the instrumental case for learning live service delivery is not meaningfully eroded by more capable drafting or documentation tools.

A decade out, service robots and AI-mediated guest interfaces (chatbots, kiosks, automated check-in) will likely handle more routine, scriptable service touchpoints, and that is a genuine capability trend worth naming rather than dismissing outright. But the specific competence this course builds — a human reading and responding to nonverbal, culturally inflected, real-time guest needs, and training others to do so in a live service environment — sits outside what those systems perform, and the central case does not have AI substituting for the embodied service-delivery judgment itself by 2036. The rating stays Low; the honest caveat is that the surrounding service-delivery landscape, including front-desk and reservation touchpoints, may automate around this human core faster than the instrumental necessity of personally learning it disappears.
HTE 1041.d: This course covers aspects of interpersonal, intercultural and nonverbal components of service to the customer. Students will examine the cycle of service, critical points of service, various customer service systems, methods used to evaluate customer service systems and effective training and development for delivery of successful customer service.

r: The course covers the operational, managerial, and legal dimensions of running a gaming or casino business: compliance frameworks, operational structure, and management practice specific to the industry. These map to analytical and interpretive Generalized Work Activities — evaluating information against regulatory standards, guiding operations — that observed-usage data shows concentrated in the Computer & Mathematical and business-analysis usage categories. Gaming-specific regulatory compliance carries some real error cost, giving modest verification weight, but the content is not embodied and carries no licensure or accreditation lock of its own, unlike the state gaming licenses individual operators must hold. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI already drafts competent compliance summaries and operational analysis, but adoption in this specialized niche remains limited and the applied managerial judgment retains near-term value.

By 2031, AI will competently synthesize gaming-regulatory frameworks, draft compliance documentation, and support operational and financial analysis for casino management, and the applied managerial-knowledge tasks this course teaches will be broadly reproducible. Macro-level productivity estimates suggest aggregate displacement remains modest even as individual task capability accelerates, but at the level of this specific course's content, no embodiment, licensure, or foundational lock caps the rating past the near term. The rating rises to High: the analytical and regulatory-interpretation work is performed competently by AI with limited human input, while the residual — signing off on regulatory filings and exercising accountable managerial judgment in a state-licensed industry — is real but narrower than the course's full operational and legal content taken together.

A decade out, AI is embedded in casino operations analytics, compliance monitoring, and reporting, and the instrumental case for a course teaching students to perform that analysis manually is substantially eroded. The rating holds High, hedged by ten-year uncertainty about how heavily state gaming commissions will continue to require demonstrable human accountability in licensed operations — a governance question distinct from raw AI capability and one this rating cannot resolve on capability evidence alone. The direction is clear: routine compliance and operational analysis automate, while accountable human sign-off in a state-licensed industry persists as a narrower residual than the course's full managerial and legal content, which is why the rating tracks the exposed business courses rather than the protected licensure-gated ones.
HTE 1052.d: This course introduces the student to a thorough understanding of the operational, management, and legal aspects of the gaming and casino industry business.

r: The applied work is preparing and analyzing hospitality-specific accounting outputs — balance sheets, income statements, cash-flow statements under the Uniform System of Accounts — and performing budgeting, forecasting, pricing, and revenue-management analysis via case work. These are quantitative, spreadsheet-based tasks squarely inside the Computer & Mathematical usage category that observed-usage data shows dominates current AI use, and GDPval benchmarks already show frontier models approaching parity with human experts on real financial-analysis deliverables. No accreditation credit-hour lock binds this course (unlike the CPA-track ACC sequence it builds on), and the content is fully digital with no embodiment. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI competently performs much of this analysis already, though classroom and firm-level adoption of AI-driven revenue management is still uneven.

By 2031, AI will competently prepare hospitality financial statements, run budgeting and forecasting models, and generate pricing and revenue-management recommendations directly from case data — precisely the applied tasks this course's knowledge serves. Productivity research on professional analytical writing shows large time savings alongside quality gains when AI drafts and a human reviews, a pattern that generalizes readily to managerial-accounting case analysis of the kind this course assigns. No CPA credit-hour requirement, licensure, or embodiment protects this hospitality-specific course the way it protects the general accounting sequence feeding the CPA pathway. The rating rises to High: the applied financial-analysis and revenue-management execution is substantially reproducible by AI with limited human input, leaving interpretive judgment on ambiguous, high-stakes pricing decisions as the narrower residual.

A decade out, AI performing hospitality financial analysis, forecasting, and dynamic pricing at production quality is the central case, and nothing in this course's institutional profile — no licensure, no accreditation credit floor, no foundational role for later required courses in this batch — holds the rating down. It stays High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty over how revenue-management practice itself restructures around automated pricing engines, which could shift the residual human role toward strategic oversight of algorithmic decisions rather than eliminating that role outright. The instrumental case for manually executing this course's calculation-heavy content is substantially eroded under the central capability trajectory, more so than for general accounting courses that retain a CPA-pathway credit-hour lock this hospitality-specific course lacks entirely.
HTE 3250.d: This course concentrates on the analysis and interpretation of hotel, restaurant, event and tourism accounting procedures and financial statements. The importance of Uniform System of Accounts for hospitality businesses, the completion of the accounting cycle, and ethical accounting practices are related to the production and analysis of: balance sheets, income statements, and cash flow statements. Principles of budgeting, forecasting, pricing techniques, revenue management, financial ratios and financial management are reviewed by conducting case analysis explicit to the hotel, restaurant, events, and tourism industries.

r: The course develops embodied culinary competence: preparing and serving cuisines from global regions using authentic ingredients and tools, alongside cultural-historical study of dining traditions, taboos, and etiquette. The hands-on preparation and service component is psychomotor and physical — knife work, cooking technique, plating, service execution — activities task-exposure research places firmly outside AI's automatable range, since a model can describe a technique but cannot develop a student's physical skill for them. The cultural-history content is more exposed to text-generation tools, but it is a supporting rather than dominant fraction of the course. No licensure or accreditation lock applies, but embodiment alone is doing the protective work here. At 24 months the instrumental need to personally acquire hands-on preparation and service technique is fully intact.

By 2031, AI will generate polished culinary-history narratives and cultural-context essays fluently, and recipe and technique documentation will be widely AI-assisted, drawing on rapid capability growth in generative content tools. That erodes the exposed minority of the course's content but leaves the central pedagogical act — a student physically preparing and plating dishes with authentic ingredients and tools, developing technique through repetition — untouched, since the jagged-frontier finding indicates AI performance degrades sharply once tasks move from text generation into physical, real-world execution. There is no embodiment substitute available at this horizon; kitchen robotics remain far from general culinary competence in an instructional setting. The rating holds Low: the psychomotor skill-building core resists substitution even as the surrounding descriptive content becomes more AI-generated.

A decade out, kitchen automation and AI-assisted recipe development will be more capable and more visible in commercial food service, a genuine capability trend worth naming rather than dismissing outright. But the specific competence Global Cuisine builds — a student's own embodied technique, sensory judgment, and hands-on service skill across diverse culinary traditions, developed through direct hands-on practice with real ingredients — is not a task performed on the learner's behalf by any foreseeable AI system; robotics adoption in general culinary education remains a market-diffusion question, not a central-case near-term reality. The rating stays Low; the honest caveat is that commercial kitchens and catering operations may automate around this skill faster than the instrumental need to personally learn it disappears.
HTE 3310.d: In this course, students explore the culinary history and development of cuisines from global, cultural perspectives. Students will study and experience cuisines from worldwide regions utilizing authentic ingredients and tools for preparation and service. An emphasis is placed on the influences that have developed cultural traditions, taboos and dining etiquette, as practiced by the global populations.

r: The course covers HR functions in hospitality organizations — planning, organizing, goal setting, recruitment, training design, and EEO and diversity compliance. Much of this knowledge work (drafting policy language, recruitment materials, training curricula, compliance summaries) is exposed to AI, and observed-usage data shows business-and-administrative tasks a growing share of current AI use. EEO and discrimination-law compliance carries real error cost, giving the course modest verification weight, and the interpersonal core — communicating effectively, managing people — provides some but not decisive protection, since it is a fraction rather than the whole of the content. No accreditation mandate binds (AACSB, where applicable, sets no course-specific requirement). At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI competently supports HR analysis and drafting, but realized classroom displacement is still partial.

By 2031, AI will handle much of the analytical and documentary work of hospitality HR — policy drafting, recruitment materials, training-program design, compliance reporting — and productivity research on professional writing shows exactly this kind of drafting task yielding large efficiency gains when AI produces a first pass. The applied tasks the course's knowledge serves become broadly automatable, and no institutional lock caps the rating past the near term. The interpersonal residue — actually motivating and coordinating people, managing conflict — is real but is a modest fraction of the course's HR-function content. The rating rises to High: the applied HR-knowledge work is performed competently by AI with limited human input for most tasks, leaving interpersonal leadership as the narrower residual.

A decade out, AI is deeply embedded in HR administration and analysis across the hospitality sector, and the instrumental case for a course teaching students to perform HR planning and documentation manually is substantially eroded, with human HR professionals concentrated on interpersonal mediation and accountable judgment calls. The rating holds High, hedged by ten-year uncertainty about how employment-law liability structures shape how much human sign-off firms continue to require on EEO and disciplinary matters regardless of AI capability, and about how heavily litigation exposure keeps a trained human formally accountable. The direction is clear: the analytical and documentary bulk of HR work automates, even as the interpersonal-leadership residue persists and is not itself the whole of what this course teaches.
HTE 3550.d: In this course, students examine the human resources and management issues that are prevalent in the hotel, restaurant, tourism, and events industries. The course explores planning, organizing, goal setting, and communicating effectively. Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO), diversity, recruitment, and training are also covered in this course.

r: The course applies marketing and advertising principles to hotel, restaurant, tourism, and event businesses, including field work analyzing and applying marketing concepts to real operations and current industry application. Marketing content generation, campaign analysis, and segmentation are among the most-exposed task categories in task-exposure research, and observed-usage data shows writing and business-analysis tasks a prominent share of current AI use. The field-work component adds a modest interpersonal and applied-judgment layer, but it is analysis and application of concepts rather than embodied service delivery, so it provides limited protection. No accreditation lock binds. At 24 months the rating is Medium: AI already drafts competent marketing copy and campaign analysis, but near-term classroom and firm-level diffusion into this specific applied field work remains partial.

By 2031, AI will competently perform the great majority of marketing execution relevant to hospitality businesses — content, campaign analysis, segmentation, positioning research — and the applied tasks this course's knowledge serves become broadly automatable. Task-exposure research consistently places marketing content generation among the most exposed activities, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational cap holds the rating down past the near term for a course with this institutional profile. The field-work and applied-analysis component migrates substantially to AI-assisted workflows as well over this horizon. The rating rises to High: the applied marketing work is performed competently by AI with limited human input, with brand strategy and client-specific judgment forming a real but narrower residual than the course's full applied-marketing content.

A decade out, AI performs nearly all marketing execution and much strategic analysis for hospitality operations, and the instrumental case for a course teaching students to perform that work manually is substantially eroded, shifting value toward strategic judgment and brand positioning held by fewer practitioners. The rating holds High, hedged by ten-year uncertainty about whether hospitality-specific brand and guest-experience judgment sustains more human marketing work than a pure capability read implies, particularly for boutique and experience-driven properties. Among the hospitality business-core courses, marketing tracks the general MKT pattern closely, since its applied output — copy, campaigns, segmentation, positioning — sits squarely in the highest-exposure task categories described by task-exposure research, with no institutional constraint here to hold the rating back.
HTE 3570.d: In this course, students apply the principles of marketing and advertising to the specific needs of the hotel, restaurant, tourism, and event industries. Students will conduct field work in their area of concentration, analyze particular marketing concepts, and provide current application.

r: The course teaches legal fundamentals applied to hospitality operations — contract law, negligence, Civil Rights compliance, food and alcohol liability, employment practice, and franchising — with an explicit preventative-management framing. AI already drafts competent legal summaries and contract language, an exposed writing task, but applying that knowledge to specific liability scenarios (was this negligence, does this contract term hold, does this practice violate Civil Rights law) carries high error cost with non-obvious failure modes, which the rating framework treats as protective verification burden. There is no bar-exam or licensure lock, since this is legal literacy for hospitality managers rather than a pre-law credential. At 24 months the rating is Low: the liability-judgment core keeps a knowledgeable human load-bearing despite exposed surrounding content.

By 2031, AI legal-research and drafting tools will handle routine contract review and compliance summarization competently, and the jagged-frontier finding is directly relevant here: outside carefully verified legal contexts, AI users show markedly lower accuracy with miscalibrated confidence, which is exactly the adversarial, liability-bearing terrain this course covers. That verification burden dampens the rating one band even as the base task-exposure of legal writing and research rises substantially. No accreditation credit floor or licensure protects the course further, and none is expected to emerge for this hospitality-legal-literacy course. The rating moves to Medium: much of the descriptive legal-fundamentals content becomes AI-reproducible, but applying it correctly to specific negligence, contract, and compliance scenarios still plausibly requires a human who understands the underlying law well enough to catch a wrong answer.

A decade out, AI legal-analysis tools will be markedly more capable at flagging liability risk and drafting compliant policy language, and the central case has much of this course's descriptive content substantially automated. What plausibly persists is the verification role — a hospitality manager who can judge when an AI-generated liability assessment is wrong before it is relied on operationally — which the deterministic rule's verification-burden dampener continues to reflect at Medium rather than High. The genuine ten-year uncertainty is how far legal-AI tools close the accuracy gap in specific, fact-dependent liability determinations; if they close it further than the central case assumes, this course's rating is the more likely candidate in this batch to drift toward High rather than staying capped by verification concerns.
HTE 3580.d: This course provides an overview of the legal fundamentals that apply to operations and management in the hospitality and tourism industries with an emphasis on preventative management practices. Legal procedures, Civil Rights, contract law, negligence, relationships with guests, and specialized liabilities related to food and alcohol service and tourism companies are covered. Additional topics of contemporary legal issues as they relate to employment practices, market regulations, and franchising.

r: HTE 3623 trains students in quantity food production, front-of-house service sequencing, garnish and plate presentation, buffet and a la carte service, sanitation protocol, food cost control, inventory procedures, and equipment operation, executed in real time on a working line and dining floor. Task-exposure research classifies manual, psychomotor, real-time interpersonal work as low-exposure, and that pattern holds directly here: no deployed AI system plates food, runs a sauté station, or manages a dining room during service. Cost control and inventory are the only sub-tasks touching software, and spreadsheet or point-of-sale tools already assist without displacing the course's applied purpose. The binding constraint is embodiment: physical execution under time pressure, with sanitation and food-safety consequences for error. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised hands-on training remains essentially unchanged.

Over five years, back-office elements of this course — recipe costing, inventory forecasting, scheduling, merchandising copy — will likely see heavier AI assistance, consistent with observed-usage data showing computer-and-office tasks as the largest current usage category. However, the course's center of gravity is laboratory production and real-world dining service: garnishing, plating, buffet execution, and guest-facing service delivery remain psychomotor and interpersonal tasks that diffusion data suggest AI adopts unevenly into physical workplaces even where firm-level AI use is spreading. Verification burden stays meaningful because sanitation and food-safety failures carry real cost and are not easily caught after the fact by a supervising instructor reviewing output. Enrollment in labor-saving kitchen technology will not substitute for a student's own competence in executing service under pressure. Expect continued Low instrumental displacement, with modest erosion confined to administrative sub-tasks rather than the course's core skill set.

At ten years, some quantity-production and cost-management workflows may be substantially software-mediated, and capability-trend evidence on rapidly lengthening AI task horizons makes larger shifts in back-of-house planning plausible, though timing is uncertain. Still, the course's defining tasks — plating, buffet and a la carte service execution, sanitation compliance, and live guest interaction — sit squarely in the embodied, real-time category that task-exposure research treats as persistently low-exposure regardless of frontier model capability, because no forecasted deployment pathway substitutes a physical body executing service in a dining room. No licensure or accreditation clock-hour mandate locks this course in place, so protection rests entirely on embodiment rather than institutional rule. This is a genuine ten-year hedge rather than a confident prediction, but the physical, in-person core of quantity food production and service is not one where instrumental need for student training plausibly collapses.
HTE 3623.d: This course is designed to teach the student how to manage quantity food production and front of the house operations through laboratory work and real-world dining experiences The student will learn culinary vocabulary, garnishing and plate presentation, buffet and a la carte dining service, work simplification, sanitation, merchandising, food cost control, inventory procedures, time management, employee management and equipment operation.

r: Garde Manger trains hot- and cold-plated food production, buffet and banquet event management, artistic showpiece construction, food-station layout and design, and live guest interaction across a la carte and banquet service. These are psychomotor, aesthetic, and real-time coordination tasks — a student sculpting an ice or tallow showpiece or running a banquet buffet line is not a task any deployed AI system performs. Task-exposure research is explicit that manual and physical craft work is low-exposure, and profit-accountability elements (costing showpieces, portion control) are the only digitally-touched sub-tasks, already assisted by ordinary spreadsheet tools without displacing the studio's purpose. The binding constraint is embodied craftsmanship under real event conditions, where presentation quality and timing are judged live. At 24 months, instrumental need for this hands-on course is essentially undiminished by current AI deployment.

By five years, AI tools may increasingly assist menu and station-layout planning, recipe scaling, and event-costing spreadsheets, mirroring observed-usage patterns where office and planning tasks see the heaviest uptake. But the studio's core — producing a showpiece, executing hot- and cold-plated presentation, and physically running a buffet or banquet station under time and guest pressure — remains embodied craft work that diffusion data suggest lags well behind capability even as firm AI adoption grows. Verification burden is real: a showpiece or plated dish either meets professional presentation standards or it does not, and that judgment is made in person, not through review of AI output. No licensure structure protects this course, so its Low rating rests entirely on the embodied, presentation-judged nature of the work, which is not expected to erode substantially within five years.

At ten years, planning-adjacent tasks around Garde Manger — costing, layout drafting, trend research for showpiece design — could be meaningfully AI-assisted given the pace implied by capability-trend evidence on lengthening task horizons, but the studio activity itself is defined by hand skill, artistic execution, and live banquet coordination that has no clear digital substitute in any forecasted deployment path. Task-exposure research's treatment of manual, real-time craft work as persistently low-exposure is the strongest anchor available for a decade-out judgment, and no institutional or licensure lock is needed to explain the protection because embodiment does the work on its own. This is offered as a hedge, not a confident forecast, but a course whose deliverable is a guest-facing, physically constructed showpiece is not plausibly replaced by AI performing the applied task itself.
HTE 3833.d: This course immerses the student in the art and science of garde manger cuisine that emphasizes hot- and cold-plated foods, buffets, showpieces, current plating trends, and profit accountability. Students will produce and manage all aspects of a la carte and banquet events to include front-of-the-house buffet design, artistic showpieces, layout and design of food stations, and guest interactions.

r: This internship places students in an approved hospitality, tourism, or events worksite under a tripartite learning contract with faculty and site supervisors, converting 50 clock hours of on-site work into one credit hour. The applied tasks are whatever the host site assigns — event coordination, guest services, operations support — but the course's instrumental value is the supervised, real-world performance of a job role, not a discrete cognitive task an AI model could complete on the student's behalf. Task-exposure research's low-exposure classification for manual and in-person interpersonal work applies directly to on-site hospitality labor. The binding constraint is structural rather than technological: a learning contract requires physical presence and supervisor evaluation, which no AI substitute satisfies. At 24 months, instrumental need for supervised placement is unaffected by current AI deployment.

Over five years, individual tasks within a given internship placement — scheduling software, guest correspondence drafting, reporting — may see AI assistance, consistent with observed-usage data on office-task uptake, and some host employers may adopt AI tools the intern is expected to use competently. That shifts what students do on-site without displacing the course's structural purpose: a learning contract tied to physical clock hours at an approved site under supervisor evaluation. Diffusion data indicate firm-level AI adoption remains well under half of US businesses, so many host sites will still run largely human-staffed operations. Verification burden is inherent to internship design, since a faculty and site supervisor jointly assess performance rather than reviewing model output. The course's Low rating should hold, contingent on hospitality operations continuing to require staffed, on-site labor at placement sites.

At ten years, it is plausible that some hospitality operations functions interns are placed into will be reorganized around AI-assisted workflows, and capability-trend evidence on how quickly AI task horizons are lengthening makes larger shifts to job content at host sites reasonable to anticipate, though which functions and how fast is genuinely uncertain. The course structure itself — a 50-clock-hour learning contract with faculty and site supervision — is defined by physical presence and supervised performance rather than task content, so its instrumental need is comparatively insulated from task-level automation even if the substance of intern duties changes considerably. This is a hedge, not a forecast: if host industries restructure toward far leaner, AI-mediated staffing models, the internship's practical placement value could erode, but no evidence available today supports assigning that outcome high confidence.
HTE 3980.d: This internship requires specialized skills that students may apply in hospitality, tourism and events settings. A written learning contract between student, faculty supervisor, site supervisor, agency, and department chair is required. Activities include finding and working in an approved hospitality, tourism or events setting. Academic credit is determined according to a ratio of 50 clock hours worked as equivalent to 1 credit hour. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: Hospitality Field Experience requires 30 hours of supervised field placement in an internship, community volunteer program, or study-abroad setting, applying theoretical hospitality and tourism concepts to a practical on-site learning experience for students who have completed twelve hours in their concentration and reached senior standing. Like other placement-based courses, its instrumental value lies in physically situated, supervised performance rather than in a task an AI model completes. Task-exposure research's classification of manual and in-person interpersonal roles as low-exposure applies to field placements in operations, guest services, or community settings. The binding constraint is structural: hour-based field presence supervised by faculty or a site contact, which has no AI equivalent. At 24 months, instrumental need for this experiential requirement is unaffected by current AI capability or deployment.

Over five years, the specific tasks students perform during their 30 hours of field placement may increasingly involve AI-assisted tools at the host site, consistent with observed-usage data showing broad uptake of AI in office and coordination work, and study-abroad or community settings will vary widely in how much AI mediates daily operations. What does not change is the course's structural requirement: a set number of physically logged hours in a real setting, evaluated through direct experience rather than digital output. Diffusion evidence indicates AI adoption across firms remains a minority practice even late in this window, so many placement sites will still be substantially human-run. Verification of learning here happens through supervised, embodied experience, not through checking model outputs, which keeps the course's Low rating comparatively stable at the five-year horizon.

At ten years, it is possible that some placement settings — particularly office-adjacent hospitality operations — will look substantially different due to AI-mediated workflows, and capability-trend evidence on the pace of AI task-horizon growth supports taking that possibility seriously rather than dismissing it. But the field-experience requirement is defined by physically accruing supervised hours in an operating, community, or international setting, a structural design that does not depend on any particular task remaining unautomated. No licensure or accreditation clock-hour mandate specifically locks this course, so its protection is functional rather than regulatory. This is a hedge rather than a confident prediction: if field placements themselves become scarce or fully virtualized, the calculus would change, but nothing in the available evidence points toward that outcome as the more likely one.
HTE 4000.d: In this course, students apply the theoretical concepts of hospitality and tourism to a practical, on-site, learning experience. The course includes 30 hours of field experience in an internship, community volunteer program, or a study-abroad setting.

r: Hospitality Senior Research teaches seniors to analyze and synthesize a research need, develop a major research project in hospitality, tourism, or events, and interpret results for application to their concentration — tasks centered on literature synthesis, methodology design, data interpretation, and written argument. These are cognitive, largely digital activities, and task-exposure research finds writing and analytical synthesis positively associated with AI exposure, while observed-usage data show computer-and-office work as the dominant current usage category. Even so, verification burden is real at this stage: students are learning to judge methodological validity and interpret findings correctly, a skill an AI-drafted literature review or analysis cannot substitute for without expert oversight catching errors. That verification need is the binding constraint at 24 months, holding the rating below what raw task content alone would suggest.

By five years, AI assistance with literature synthesis, drafting, and even preliminary data analysis is likely to be substantially more capable and more routinely used, consistent with capability-trend evidence on rapidly lengthening AI task horizons and with GDPval findings that top models are already approaching parity with human experts on realistic deliverables in analytical domains. The course's tasks — synthesizing sources, structuring a research project, interpreting results — sit closer to the programming-and-writing cluster that task-exposure research associates with higher exposure than to the science-and-critical-thinking cluster it treats as protective. Verification burden eases somewhat as tools improve, though it does not disappear given the jagged-frontier finding that users outside a model's competence area misjudge accuracy. No licensure lock applies. Expect a rating shift toward Medium as instrumental need for unaided synthesis and drafting narrows.

At ten years, a senior research capstone built primarily on literature synthesis, data interpretation, and written argument sits in territory where task-exposure research's positive association between writing and programming tasks and AI exposure, combined with GDPval evidence of near-parity performance on realistic deliverables, points toward substantial instrumental displacement of the drafting and synthesis work itself. No foundational-scaffolding or licensure constraint locks this course in place, since it is a terminal capstone rather than a prerequisite for further required coursework. The hedge is real, however: capability trends are extrapolated from a few years of data, and what counts as adequate synthesis and interpretation for degree purposes is a curricular choice, not solely a technical one. On current evidence, though, this is a course where high instrumental displacement is a defensible ten-year expectation rather than an overreach.
HTE 4040.d: This course provides the approaches and techniques necessary for senior students to analyze and synthesize-needs, create and develop a major research project in Hospitality, Tourism, and Events, and effectively interpret results and their application to their major concentration area.

r: Current Topics: Lodging is a seminar-style elective surveying changing trends and problems in the hotel industry alongside career and personal development topics, built around discussion, case examples, and instructor-curated current material rather than fixed textbook content. This is cognitive, discussion-based work: task-exposure research associates this kind of synthesis and communication activity with meaningful AI exposure, and observed-usage data show substantial current uptake for office and knowledge tasks generally. Verification burden matters here because current-topics content changes quickly and requires an instructor's judgment about what is actually accurate and industry-relevant, a role AI-generated trend summaries cannot fully replace without expert curation. That verification need is the binding constraint at 24 months. No licensure or accreditation mandate protects this elective, so its rating tracks task content directly rather than institutional lock-in.

By five years, AI-generated industry trend synthesis and case-example compilation are likely to be considerably more capable and more routinely produced, consistent with capability-trend evidence on how quickly AI task horizons are lengthening and with observed-usage data showing heavy uptake for research and writing-adjacent tasks. A seminar built on current topics is, in content-generation terms, close to tasks task-exposure research associates with higher exposure — synthesizing and communicating rapidly changing information — rather than the science-and-critical-thinking cluster it treats as protective. Verification burden eases as retrieval-grounded tools become more reliable at tracking genuinely current, accurate industry information, though the jagged-frontier finding that misplaced trust causes real errors outside a model's competence area still counsels some caution. No licensure lock applies. Expect the rating to move toward High as instrumental need for unaided trend synthesis narrows.

At ten years, a topics seminar whose core work is synthesizing and communicating current industry information sits squarely in the higher-exposure cluster task-exposure research identifies — writing, synthesis, and communication — rather than the protected science-and-critical-thinking cluster, and capability-trend evidence on the pace of AI improvement makes it plausible that AI-curated, continuously updated trend briefings could substantially perform the instrumental function this course serves. No foundational-scaffolding role or licensure requirement locks the course in place, since it is an elective survey rather than a prerequisite. The hedge is necessary because current-topics pedagogy also has a discussion and career-development component that depends on live instructor and peer interaction, which is harder to displace than pure content synthesis. Still, on available evidence a High rating at the ten-year horizon is defensible rather than a stretch.
HTE 4592.d: The course considers various problems, subjects, and trends related to changing environments and events in the hotel industry. Subjects related to career as well as personal development may also be studied.

r: Hospitality Negotiations and Sales covers the legal, ethical, and practical environment of meeting-contract negotiation and event execution, teaching negotiation and sales strategy for representing contracted events. Contract language review and sales-material drafting are text-based tasks AI already assists with, but live negotiation — reading a counterpart, adapting strategy in real time, building trust that closes a deal — is real-time interpersonal work that task-exposure research treats as comparatively low-exposure. Verification burden is elevated because a negotiated meeting contract carries binding legal and financial consequences, and an error is costly and not always obvious until the event or dispute occurs, meaning expert human review remains necessary. That combination of live interpersonal execution and high-stakes contract accuracy is the binding constraint. At 24 months, instrumental need for supervised negotiation practice remains essentially intact.

Over five years, contract drafting, clause comparison, and sales-pitch preparation will likely see heavier AI assistance, tracking observed-usage data on strong uptake for writing and office tasks and productivity-RCT findings that professional writing tasks see meaningful time savings with AI support. But the negotiation itself — the live, adversarial back-and-forth where a hospitality sales professional reads a client, adjusts terms, and closes — remains real-time interpersonal work that is harder to displace, and the jagged-frontier finding that AI users misjudge accuracy outside a model's competence area is a relevant caution for high-stakes contract negotiation specifically. Verification burden stays elevated given the binding financial and legal consequences of a bad clause. No licensure lock protects the course, so its Low rating rests on embodiment and verification burden rather than institutional rule, and should hold at five years with only incremental softening.

At ten years, drafting and preparatory sub-tasks around negotiation could be substantially AI-mediated given capability-trend evidence on lengthening task horizons, and some earlier-stage sales communication may shift meaningfully toward AI assistance. Live, high-stakes negotiation itself, however, is a harder case: task-exposure research's treatment of real-time interpersonal work as comparatively protected, combined with the elevated verification burden of legally binding contracts, argues against assuming the applied skill this course teaches becomes instrumentally unnecessary. No licensure or accreditation lock is available to anchor the ten-year judgment, so the rating leans on task content itself, and a modest upward shift toward Medium reflects genuine uncertainty about how much of negotiation preparation and low-stakes deal-making becomes AI-assisted rather than confidence that live negotiation skill training becomes unnecessary.
HTE 4730.d: This course provides an overview of the legal, ethical, and practical environment which impacts the negotiation of meeting contract and the execution of the events in which they represent. It examples the strategies of negotiation and sales.

r: Hospitality Leadership has students complete self-assessments of their management and leadership styles, study leadership theory, charisma, and ethics, and investigate power, social responsibility, and politics in hotel, restaurant, tourism, and event contexts through role play and debate. The theory content is text-based and already AI-summarizable, but the course's applied core — self-assessment of one's own traits, live role play, and debate — is inherently personal and interpersonal, requiring a student's own reflective and real-time performance rather than a task an AI model completes on their behalf. Task-exposure research treats this kind of real-time interpersonal and reflective work as comparatively low-exposure. Verification burden is also present because leadership self-insight and debate performance are evaluated through live observation, not reviewable output. That combination is the binding constraint at 24 months, holding the rating low.

By five years, leadership-theory content delivery and background reading may be increasingly supplemented by AI-generated summaries, consistent with observed-usage data on strong uptake for knowledge-synthesis tasks, but the pedagogical core of this course is experiential: self-assessment, role play, and debate performed live among peers. Task-exposure research's classification of real-time interpersonal and reflective activity as comparatively low-exposure continues to apply, and no current or foreseeable AI tool completes a student's self-assessment or performs their debate role for them in any instrumentally meaningful sense. Verification burden remains elevated because leadership development is judged through direct observation of behavior rather than a checkable output. No licensure lock is relevant here. The rating should hold at Low across the five-year horizon, with only the supporting theory content seeing meaningful AI-assisted delivery.

At ten years, even as capability-trend evidence points toward AI systems handling more knowledge-delivery and theoretical-summary functions, the leadership course's defining activities — self-assessment, role play, and debate — remain tasks a student must personally perform and be observed performing, which is not the kind of task substitution the underlying automation question addresses. Task-exposure research's treatment of real-time interpersonal and self-reflective work as comparatively protected supports extending that judgment forward, though with appropriate humility about a decade-long horizon. No licensure or accreditation lock is available to anchor this further, so the hedge rests entirely on the embodied, personal nature of the coursework. Barring a fundamental redefinition of what leadership development means pedagogically, instrumental need for this experiential course appears likely to remain Low even at the ten-year mark.
HTE 4750.d: In this course, students explore theoretical findings concerning leadership and brings them to life through practical application. Students complete a series of self assessment to identify their management and leadership styles and traits. The course addresses the importance of leadership, charisma and characteristics of leaders. The meaning of ethics, social responsibility, power, and politics in the hotel, restaurant, tourism, and event industries are investigated through role play and debate.

r: Strategic Management for Hospitality has students analyze strategic-management approaches using current hotel, restaurant, tourism, and events cases, compare techniques for acquiring and managing people, knowledge, financial capital, and physical assets, and evaluate strategies for restructuring, entrepreneurship, innovation, organization design, and global alliances — a case-based, analytical capstone with corequisites spanning the program's finance, marketing, and operations core. This is cognitive, largely digital work: task-exposure research associates analytical synthesis and writing with meaningful AI exposure, and observed-usage data show strong current uptake for exactly this kind of case analysis and strategy-document drafting. Verification burden is moderate rather than severe — strategic recommendations are coursework reviewed by faculty rather than binding real-world decisions — so it does not strongly dampen the rating. No licensure lock applies. At 24 months, this converges with other business-strategy coursework at a Medium rating.

By five years, case analysis, strategy-framework application, and drafting of strategic recommendations are likely to be substantially AI-assisted, consistent with capability-trend evidence on rapidly lengthening AI task horizons and GDPval findings that top models are approaching parity with human experts on realistic analytical deliverables. As a capstone integrating finance, marketing, and operations concentrations, this course's tasks resemble the case-based strategic analysis work that generalist business courses already show elevated exposure for. Verification burden remains moderate — a flawed AI-assisted analysis is a grading issue rather than a high-stakes error — which does not meaningfully dampen the trajectory. No licensure or accreditation credit-hour mandate constrains this course. Expect a shift toward High as the instrumental value of unaided case analysis and strategy-document construction narrows relative to AI-assisted alternatives.

At ten years, a strategy capstone built on case analysis, resource-management comparison, and evaluation of restructuring, innovation, and alliance strategies sits in territory where capability-trend evidence on the pace of AI improvement and GDPval's near-parity findings on realistic business deliverables both point toward substantial instrumental displacement of the analytical and drafting work itself. No foundational-scaffolding role protects the course since it is terminal by design, and no licensure or accreditation mandate locks it in place. The hedge that remains is pedagogical rather than technical: strategic judgment developed through case debate and synthesis may retain instructional value even if AI can produce comparable analytical output, but that is a curricular argument, not evidence against exposure. On current evidence, a High rating at the ten-year horizon is defensible for this analytically-oriented capstone.
HTE 4800.d: In this course, students analyze various approaches to strategic management in a hospitality and related industry context. Course content overviews strategy concepts and ideas while illustrating relevant examples from current hotel, restaurant, tourism, and events industry cases. Student compare managerial techniques to acquire, develop, and manage internal resources such as people, knowledge, financial capital, and physical assets. Strategies for restructuring, entrepreneurship, innovation, organization design, and global alliances are analyzed to best suit stakeholder interest in hospitality and related industry businesses.

r: HTE 4860 asks students to conduct a hospitality-specific risk assessment survey, draft a loss prevention management plan, and apply legal and regulatory concepts to security operations through case studies, role playing, and site visits. Today, generative tools can competently draft portions of a loss-prevention report or synthesize case-study findings, mapping onto Getting Information and Documenting/Recording Information work activities, but the course's core deliverable requires physically walking a property, observing operational vulnerabilities, and interacting with staff and guests in role-play scenarios — tasks squarely in Inspecting Equipment, Structures, or Materials and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. Diffusion data show adoption inside hospitality operations remains uneven this early, and the safety/legal stakes of an incomplete risk survey keep the verification burden high, since an AI-drafted plan overlooking a real hazard carries direct liability exposure that a novice cannot catch unassisted.

By 2031, capability-trend research on lengthening task-time horizons suggests AI systems will more fluently produce complete draft risk-assessment surveys and loss-prevention plans, and adoption within hospitality risk-management functions should be broader than today even though industry-wide AI diffusion still lags behind raw capability. This pushes the analytical and documentation components of the course — Analyzing Data or Information, Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance with Standards — further toward automatability. However, the course's embodied core does not shift with model capability: site visits demand physical inspection of a real property's security posture, and role-playing exercises rehearse real-time interpersonal judgment under simulated emergencies, both resistant to digital substitution. Verification burden also stays elevated, because a flawed security plan implicates guest safety and legal liability that a hospitality manager, not an AI system, must ultimately certify and stand behind before implementation across an operating property.

A ten-year projection is necessarily uncertain, but if compute and capability continue compounding at anything near recent rates, AI assistance for drafting compliance-oriented risk documentation and synthesizing case precedent could become close to routine, nudging realized task automatability higher still. Even so, the course's defining activities — physically walking a property to inspect security and safety conditions, and rehearsing crisis or guest-incident scenarios through role play — remain tied to embodied, real-time human presence that no forecast currently extends to AI, so this protective floor likely persists regardless of model progress. The verification burden argument also holds over this horizon: task-exposure research associates science and critical-thinking-heavy, high-stakes judgment work with lower exposure, and a hospitality security plan that misjudges a real hazard carries consequences an unsupervised model output cannot be trusted to absorb, so a human risk professional remains the certifying authority.

Legal concepts specific to industry operations are applied in detail through case studies, role playing, and site visits.
